analysis.one_liner: Removes the liability cap so offshore oil companies pay all costs of spills they cause.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee with no hearing or vote, one of many liability proposals introduced after the 2010 Gulf oil spill.
analysis.plain_summary: Under the Oil Pollution Act of 1990, an offshore oil facility's owner must pay all oil removal costs, but its other liability — damages to fishermen, coastal businesses, and local governments — is capped at $75 million. This bill, introduced in the weeks after the Deepwater Horizon rig explosion, would delete that cap (except for deepwater ports), so the company responsible for a spill pays unlimited damages. It also made the change retroactive to April 15, 2010. The bill never left the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Coastal residents, commercial fishermen, tourism businesses, and local governments who suffer losses from an oil spill, plus federal and state taxpayers, who currently cover spill costs above the responsible party's cap.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the Oil Pollution Act's liability limitation, which currently limits a responsible offshore party's liability beyond removal costs to $75 million [S2].
Makes the responsible party fully liable for damages from a discharge, or a substantial threat of a discharge, from an offshore facility, with an exception only for deepwater ports [S2].
Sets the effective date at April 15, 2010, days before the Deepwater Horizon disaster, so the repeal would apply to that spill [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Offshore oil and gas companies, which would face unlimited liability for spill damages instead of the $75 million cap, and would likely pay more for insurance to cover that exposure.

drawbacks.text: Unlimited liability could push some smaller operators toward insolvency after a major spill, potentially leaving cleanup costs unpaid anyway, and would raise insurance and operating costs that could squeeze marginal producers out of the market.

The $75 million cap is paired with an industry-financed Oil Spill Liability Trust Fund that pays cleanup and damages up to about $1 billion; unlimited operator liability raises the question of how much responsibility properly sits with the operator versus a shared industry fund.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is straightforward: a $75 million cap is trivially small against the cost of a major spill, so without repeal, losses above the cap fall on fishermen, coastal businesses, and taxpayers. The main cost falls on oil companies, in higher insurance and liability exposure, which is the point of the bill. The strongest good-faith objection is that unlimited liability can be difficult to insure against and may not actually collect money from an insolvent operator, but that is an argument for stronger financial-responsibility rules, not for keeping the cap.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and then to two subcommittees, and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Raúl Grijalva introduced the bill on May 20, 2010 [S1].
The House referred it to the Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure the day it was introduced [S5].
The next day it was referred to the Subcommittee on Water Resources and Environment and the Subcommittee on Coast Guard and Maritime Transportation, and no further action was ever taken [S5].
Nineteen House Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republicans did [S4].
The bill's effective date was set at April 15, 2010, retroactive to before the Deepwater Horizon disaster of April 20, 2010 [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Offshore oil and gas companies, which kept the $75 million liability cap and left spill damages beyond it to be absorbed by coastal communities and taxpayers.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Offshore oil companies kept the liability cap

for.name: Raúl M. Grijalva
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the offshore liability cap on May 20, 2010.

against.name: House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill, referred it to two subcommittees, and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on it.

against.name: Offshore oil and gas industry
against.role: Industry opposed to lifting or removing the liability cap
against.what_they_did: Opposed proposals to raise or eliminate the Oil Pollution Act liability cap after the Deepwater Horizon spill.

sides.party_line_note: All 19 cosponsors, like the sponsor, were House Democrats; no Republicans signed on and no vote was ever taken, so opposition shows up only as committee inaction.

industries.note: The bill would strip the $75 million cap on their liability for spill damages, making them pay full cleanup and compensation costs. Their interest in keeping the cap runs against the public, because spill losses above the cap fall on coastal communities and taxpayers.

industries.industry: Commercial fishing and coastal tourism businesses
industries.note: These businesses suffer the bulk of spill damages beyond the cap; full liability for the responsible party would give them a solvent source of compensation.

industries.industry: Marine insurance and P&I insurers for offshore operators
industries.note: Unlimited operator liability would require substantially more liability coverage, expanding insurers' offshore business while raising operators' costs.
